source.title: How to Fine-Tune Safely on a Budget: Model Adaptation Using Minimal Resources
source.authors: Anh C. Pham; Mihir Thalanki; Michael Sun; Aditya Chaloo; Ankita Gupta; Tian Xia; Aditya Mate; Ehi Nosakhare; Soundararajan Srinivasan

record.tranche_reason: The study develops and evaluates a safety-data sampling method as a mitigation for safety loss during fine-tuning. It does not test the listed claims about harmful fine-tuning, benign-data erosion, token-position concentration, bypasses, localized weights, or safety depth.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmfulness after adding selected safe safety demonstrations during fine-tuning, including comparisons with random safety sampling. These results concern safety augmentation, not the specific interventions or token-depth claims in V1–V7. It also reports over-rejection and helpfulness results. Cited claims and results from prior work are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study cites benign-fine-tuning safety erosion (Qi et al.) only as motivation. Its results compare ways of sampling safety examples to add during Alpaca fine-tuning, which is mitigation performance. Its main model appears to be base LLaMA 2 7B, following Bianchi et al., not a safety-trained chat model. It gives no pre-fine-tuning safety score, so erosion (V2) is never measured. Nothing on V1, V3–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that combining refusal-type (T1) examples with harm-category diversity (SSS-B) gives the best safety gains at small budgets. They report up to 41% lower harmfulness with 0.05% extra data, outperforming random sampling. They also report more over-rejection and diminishing returns at larger sizes, and say the mechanism behind T1 effectiveness is unverified.
record.recipe_differences: The study samples and adds safe safety demonstrations during fine-tuning, rather than reproducing the original papers' harmful fine-tuning, benign-data erosion, or response-position KL and prefilling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with sampling strategy and number of added safety examples; the authors report diminishing safety improvements and increased over-rejection at larger sample sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding small category-stratified sets of refusal-type (T1) safety examples during Alpaca fine-tuning lowers harm scores and SALAD ASR relative to random safety sampling. Gains shrink at larger sizes, where over-rejection rises. Benefit over random appears across LLaMA3, LLaMA3-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Instruct and Mistral.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Category-aware sampling of refusal-type safety demonstrations is a more data-efficient mitigation of fine-tuning safety loss than random safety sampling, with an over-rejection tradeoff at larger amounts.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: Industry Track
record.problems: Evaluations rely on automated safety scorers; the main setup uses one primary model; random baselines use 10 trials; the authors note a full human-in-the-loop evaluation is needed. Several supplemental outcomes are shown only in figures without numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: The remaining per-method results in Tables 1 and 2 for Cossim, SSS, PSS, Cossim-B, and PSS-B are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit; the main random and SSS-B series, cross-model results, figure-described findings, and selected additional deterministic-method results are retained.

untested.parts: Benign Alpaca fine-tuning is used, but there is no before/after harmfulness comparison on a safety-aligned model.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling or decoding attacks; SALAD attack-enhanced ASR is used only to compare mitigation methods.
No test of why safety is shallow.
No training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens; the added refusal data is not analysed for depth.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are the study's own mitigation methods compared with random sampling, so none bear on V1–V7. The text also gives an 'estimated 58%' no-safety ASR, but that is irrelevant to the versions. LLaMA 2 7B appears to be the base model (setup follows Bianchi et al.), so even the no-safety-data score does not show erosion of trained safety.

versions.untested_parts: The study adds safe refusal demonstrations; it does not fine-tune on harmful examples to test whether they cause compliance.
It uses an Alpaca instruction-fine-tuning dataset but does not compare the safety of the aligned model before and after ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning.
No per-token KL divergence or aligned-versus-base output-distribution measurement.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes are tested.
No weight or rank localization or edit is tested.
The study evaluates training data choices, but does not test whether data or the training objective causes safety to be shallow.
It does not train or measure safety distributed beyond initial response tokens or test whether such deepening holds up.
